strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in generative image editing: removing target objects together with their visual effects (e.g., cast shadows and reflections) given only the target object mask.

Well-designed dataset curation pipeline (OBER) combining real counterfactual image pairs with physically grounded simulated data (using surface flatness checks, shadow direction clustering, and alpha compositing), filling a notable gap in publicly accessible object-effect removal benchmarks.

The Object-Effect Attention (OEA) mechanism and subsequent Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) are technically well-motivated: supervising cross-attention enables the model to identify the spatial extent of effects beyond the object mask, which also provides an adaptive mask for non-destructive background blending during inference.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple benchmarks (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild), demonstrating clear improvements over current state-of-the-art inpainting and removal baselines, supported by a user study, robustness analyses to user scribbles, and extensions to object insertion and repositioning.
weaknesses: The alpha map calculation in Eq. (1), defined as $(I_{gt} - I_{in}) / (I_{gt} + \varepsilon)$, strictly assumes shadows where $I_{in} \le I_{gt}$. It is not mathematically well-defined for specular reflections or bright lighting highlights where $I_{in} > I_{gt}$ (yielding negative alpha values). A clearer mathematical formulation or explanation of how reflections and additive effects are handled during RGBA compositing is needed.

A significant portion of the quantitative gain in PSNR and PSNR-BG stems directly from Attention-Guided Fusion (Table 2 shows PSNR jumps from 28.00 to 32.98 when AG Fusion is enabled), as background pixels outside the predicted mask are pasted directly from the input. While baselines were evaluated with both object masks and object-effect masks, it is not fully clear whether baselines also received post-hoc copy-paste background replacement outside their respective masks to ensure a completely fair comparison on background reconstruction metrics.

Ground truth effect masks $M_{fg}$ for real captured pairs are derived from pixel-wise intensity thresholding of $(I_{in} - I_{gt})$. In real-world capture setups, minor illumination fluctuations, subtle global exposure drift, or camera micro-movements can introduce noise or spurious boundary artifacts into the generated ground-truth effect masks.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: addressing the ubiquitous issue where diffusion-based inpainting either leaves lingering object effects (shadows, reflections) or degrades unaffected background content.

Valuable dataset contribution: OBER provides a rigorous hybrid data pipeline combining 2,715 camera-captured counterfactual pairs with 10,000 simulated pairs generated via depth-guided surface filtering, shadow clustering, and alpha compositing, with separate object and effect annotations.

Effective and elegant method design: leveraging CLIP visual object embeddings in cross-attention and supervising the attention maps with effect masks (OEA) successfully teaches the network to localize effect regions, which simultaneously enables Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) at test time to avoid background degradation.

Comprehensive empirical validation: the method is evaluated on both real and simulated benchmarks (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild) under both object-only and object+effect mask settings, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines qualitatively and quantitatively, supplemented by a user study and ablations.
weaknesses: Disentangling the contribution of AG Fusion: Table 2 shows that AG Fusion accounts for the largest quantitative leap (PSNR increases from 28.00 dB to 32.98 dB). While combining copy-paste blending with the predicted mask is practically sensible, this large jump is partly a natural consequence of preserving untouched original pixels. A dedicated evaluation isolating synthesis fidelity strictly within the ground-truth effect/removal area (e.g., masked PSNR/LPIPS inside $M_{fg}$) would give a clearer picture of generation quality versus background retention.

Formulation and stability of the attention loss: The loss is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{mask} = \text{mean}(A[1 - M_{fg}]) - \text{mean}(A[M_{fg}])$. Because cross-attention maps are typically softmax-normalized across spatial positions, this linear difference could be unbounded or sensitive to hyperparameters. More implementation details on loss weighting, layer selection, and training stability would strengthen reproducibility.

Comparison with modular baseline alternatives: The baselines tested are primarily end-to-end inpainting/editing diffusion models. Comparing against a natural two-stage baseline—such as an off-the-shelf shadow/reflection detector (e.g., DESOBA-v2 or SAM-based expansion) followed by SDXL-Inpainting—would better demonstrate the necessity and benefit of joint end-to-end attention guidance over modular pipelines.

Handling of overlapping and complex effects: As noted in the limitations, the method struggles when shadows from multiple objects overlap or when effects extend over long distances, occasionally causing incomplete removal or boundary artifacts.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in image editing: removing objects along with their associated visual effects (such as cast shadows and reflections) given only the primary object mask.

Valuable dataset contribution: The hybrid OBER dataset combines carefully captured real counterfactual pairs and simulated composite data with fine-grained masks for both objects and their visual effects, which helps address the lack of public benchmark data in this domain.

The combination of Object-Effect Attention (OEA) supervision and Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) provides an effective mechanism to localize affected areas dynamically and preserve unaffected background details during inference.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Demonstrates consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over multiple competitive baselines (e.g., PowerPaint, DesignEdit, RORem, Attentive Eraser) across multiple datasets, supported by an ablation study and human perceptual evaluation.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: supervising cross-attention maps with spatial masks is well-established in localized generation/editing (e.g., FastComposer, PortraitBooth), and using thresholded/blurred attention maps as blending masks during inference is an intuitive post-processing heuristic.

The dramatic quantitative boost in Table 2 (Exp. c vs. d, where PSNR increases from 28.00 to 32.98 and PSNR-BG to 35.14) is largely driven by pasting unmodified original pixels outside the attention mask. It remains unclear how much baseline methods would improve if paired with an external shadow/effect detector followed by standard boundary-blended inpainting.

Lack of standalone evaluation for the predicted attention masks: While recall is briefly referenced in Figure 6, a standard segmentation evaluation (e.g., IoU, precision, boundary F-score) comparing the attention-derived effect masks against ground-truth effect annotations is missing.

Eq. (1) provides an approximate formulation for alpha map estimation of effect areas that assumes simplified linear attenuation. While practical for data simulation, this formulation can break down in complex non-linear lighting conditions or specular reflections, requiring manual intervention as acknowledged in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical visual editing challenge: removing foreground objects along with their associated physical visual effects (e.g., shadows and reflections) while faithfully preserving the background.

The dataset contribution (OBER) is valuable and well-executed, combining carefully captured counterfactual real image pairs with a principled simulation pipeline (incorporating depth filtering, shadow direction clustering, and alpha matting) to provide explicit object-effect annotations.

The technical design of Adaptive Target-Aware Attention (ATA) and Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) is well-motivated, effectively leveraging learned cross-attention maps both for effect localization and for inference-time copy-paste background preservation to mitigate diffusion/VAE reconstruction drift.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (RORD-Val, OBER-Test/Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN) and a user study convincingly demonstrate clear quantitative and qualitative advantages over strong recent baselines.
weaknesses: The technical description of Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS) in the main text is relatively brief; the exact mathematical formulation of latent re-injection and how boundary discontinuities are handled during denoising could be detailed more clearly.

The Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) pipeline relies heavily on the quality of the predicted first-layer cross-attention map. As acknowledged in the limitations, when multiple objects share complex or overlapping shadows/reflections, attention leakage or under-segmentation could lead to abrupt blending seams or lingering effect artifacts.

The model is trained and evaluated primarily at 512x512 resolution despite using SDXL as the backbone, which is natively pre-trained on 1024x1024. Exploring the framework's scalability to native megapixel resolutions would further strengthen the practical utility.

The attention loss formulation in Eq. (2) simply takes the difference of means without explicit margin or scale normalization; an analysis of sensitivity to this loss formulation and its weighting relative to the diffusion loss is missing.

strengths: Significance and Problem Formulation: Effectively addressing visual effects (such as shadows and mirror/water reflections) in conjunction with object removal is a crucial yet often overlooked problem in diffusion-based image editing. The paper provides an end-to-end solution that takes only the object mask as input while removing both the object and its associated effects.

Comprehensive Dataset Contribution (OBER): The hybrid curation pipeline (combining 2,878 camera-captured counterfactual pairs with 10,000 realistically blended simulated pairs) is well-engineered. Annotating separate object masks, effect masks, and RGBA layers provides valuable supervisory signals that have been lacking in public benchmarks.

Well-Designed Methodology: The combination of Adaptive Target-Aware Attention (ATA) with explicit mask loss supervision, Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) for background preservation, and Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS) to avoid color drift is coherent and technically sound.

Extensive and Fair Empirical Validation: The method is comprehensively evaluated on multiple benchmarks (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN) across several metrics (PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, CLIP, DINO, ReMOVE). The paper carefully controls for fairness by providing baselines with ground-truth effect masks for blending (Table 7) and demonstrates substantial quantitative and visual improvements.

Versatility and Practical Extensions: Demonstrations on user strokes/scribbles, interactive object insertion, and controllable object movement highlight the practical versatility and robustness of the learned representations.
weaknesses: Resolution Limitations: The model is fine-tuned and evaluated at 512×512 resolution despite utilizing SDXL as the backbone, which is natively pre-trained for 1024×1024. Discussing the computational trade-offs or demonstrating scalability to higher resolutions would further strengthen the work.

Mathematical Formulation of SVDS: The Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength is conceptually intuitive but lacks formal algorithmic or mathematical formulation in Section 3.2 (e.g., explicit equations describing how latent blending and re-injection are scheduled across timesteps during inference).

Failure Modes Under Complex Illumination: As acknowledged in the limitations, the model can struggle when multiple objects cast overlapping shadows or interact under intricate multi-light setups, pointing to the inherent challenge of 2D attention-based reasoning without explicit 3D physical modeling.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addressing the visual effects (such as cast shadows and reflections) associated with an object during inpainting/removal is a critical yet challenging practical task that standard mask-based inpainting models often fail to handle cleanly.

Sound and effective methodology: Supervising cross-attention maps via Adaptive Target-Aware Attention (ATA) with ground-truth object-effect masks provides an elegant way to learn effect localization. Using the learned attention maps for Attention-Guided Fusion (AGF) at test time effectively circumvents the background degradation and color shifts typical of diffusion inpainting pipelines.

Comprehensive dataset contribution: The hybrid OBER dataset combines physically captured counterfactual image pairs (fixed camera before/after removal) with a well-reasoned simulation pipeline (using extracted alpha maps, surface flatness filtering via depth estimation, and shadow-direction clustering).

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper evaluates across numerous benchmarks (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniEraser-Bench, OmniPaint-Bench, and MULAN) and provides solid comparisons against modern baselines. Both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations demonstrate clear gains in object-effect removal and background preservation.

Thorough ablations and extensions: The paper presents clear component-wise ablations (Table 2) verifying the impact of ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS, alongside practical extensions such as user scribbles/strokes, multi-object removal, and object insertion.
weaknesses: Mathematical formulation of the attention loss: In Eq. (2), $L_{mask} = \text{mean}(A[1 - M_{fg}]) - \text{mean}(A[M_{fg}])$ is unbounded below unless the attention values $A$ are explicitly constrained or normalized across spatial locations. The manuscript lacks details on whether and how spatial softmax, clamping, or scaling is applied to $A$ during training.

Sensitivity to AGF hyperparameters: The Attention-Guided Fusion relies on taking the first-layer cross-attention map at the final denoising step, followed by upsampling and Gaussian blurring. The paper does not provide an analysis of sensitivity regarding the selection of layers, denoising steps, or the blur radius.

Formalization of SVDS: The Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength is described conceptually in Section 3.2 (applying $DS=1.0$ in the masked area and $DS=0.99$ outside via latent reinjection), but lacking explicit mathematical notation in the methodology section explaining how the latent noise schedule is blended at each reverse step.

Limitations in complex entangled lighting: As acknowledged in the limitations, when multiple objects produce intertwined or overlapping shadows/reflections, the model struggles to disentangle target effects from neighboring objects' effects, sometimes leading to under- or over-removal.
